title: Kinds of Claims
short: Claims of fact (is it so?), of value (is it good or bad?) and of policy (what should we do?).
trouble: Learners confuse a claim of value with a claim of fact because both use is (“Homework is useless” is a judgment, not a measurement).

blocks.html: On the Logic Ladder you learned to find an argument’s conclusion first. In writing, the conclusion you argue for is your claim. After the appeals, the next question is: what kind of claim is it? Claims come in three kinds, and each asks a different question.

head: Kind
Asks
Example
What you owe the reader
rows: Is it so? Was it so? Will it be so?
Most students at our school sleep less than eight hours on school nights.
evidence that it is true (a survey, records, measurements)
Is it good or bad, better or worse, right or wrong?
The 7:15 start is the worst part of our school day.
criteria for judging, then evidence that the thing meets them
The district should start high school at 8:30.
a problem, a solution, and reasons the solution will work and is worth its costs
blocks.cap: Three kinds of claims about one subject.

blocks.html: A claim of fact says what is true; a claim of value judges; a claim of policy says what should be done. Name the kind, and you know what support the claim needs.

Each kind of claim makes a different promise. A claim of fact promises evidence. A claim of value promises standards of judgment. A claim of policy promises a workable plan. Writers who mix them up give the wrong support: a pile of statistics for a value claim, or a moral judgment where the reader wanted a plan.

blocks.title: The word is can fool you
blocks.q: Is “Homework is useless” a claim of fact or of value?
steps: It uses is, like a fact. But useless is a judgment, not a measurement.
Ask: could a survey or a ruler settle it? Only after we agree what “useful” means: higher grades, better habits, more practice?
So it is a claim of value. To argue it, first set the criteria, then show homework fails them.
A related claim of fact: “Students in our survey spent an average of 70 minutes a night on homework.”
blocks.a: Value: useless is a judgment that needs criteria.

blocks.title: Claims stack up
blocks.q: An editorial argues that the town should plant trees on Main Street. Find a claim of each kind in its case.
steps: Fact: streets with trees are cooler in summer than bare streets. (Measurable.)
Value: a cooler, shadier street is better for people who walk and shop there. (A judgment.)
Policy: the town should plant trees on Main Street. (An action.)
Policy claims usually rest on claims of fact and value underneath.
blocks.a: Fact (trees cool streets), value (cooler is better for walkers), policy (plant the trees).

blocks.html: Confusing a claim of value with a claim of fact because both use is. “The new library is beautiful” and “The new library is too small” are judgments; “The new library has 40 study seats” is a fact. Check: could people agree on a way to measure it before they argue? If the argument is really about standards, it is a value claim.

cards.text: The library closes at 4:00 on weekdays.
The library’s new reading room is the best place in town to study.
The library should stay open until 8:00.
Recess is the most important part of the school day.
Our school ended recess for fifth graders in 2022.
Every elementary student ought to have at least twenty minutes of recess.
cards.why: Ought to marks a course of action.
